title: The Jest Unmade
story:
A moment before, Krishna had teased her in play, telling her she had chosen a penniless husband when she might have had any king. Rukmini had believed him and fainted. Now she came to herself in his arms, and the first thing she understood was that the world had not ended — only her certainty in it.

He had lifted her from where she fell and was wiping her tears. When he saw her eyes open, he told her the truth at last. He had spoken in jest. He had wanted to see her face, he said — the face of a woman who loved him, trembling between love and anger. That face, he told her, was worth more to a man than all the wealth of his house; nothing he owned could equal it.

She looked at him for a long moment. Then Rukmini, who had been silent, spoke — and she did not scold him. She answered the jest as if it were the most serious question ever put to her.

She knew, she said, whom she had chosen. The kings he named were mortal lords with mortal power, and she had seen what became of such kings: Anga and Vainya, Jayanta, Nahusha and Gaya had all held the whole earth and, wanting only him, had laid their kingdoms down and walked into the forest. Even the guardians of the worlds, she said, laid offerings at his feet, and sages who had put aside anger worshipped him in silence. At her own svayamvara, the ceremony where a princess chooses her husband, his bow had spoken once, and the kings had scattered like animals before a lion; he had carried her off the way a lion carries off its share. After that there was no one else she could shelter under. Having once breathed the fragrance of his feet — the fragrance that sets the sorrowful free — what other refuge would any woman choose?

Let her be a servant, she said, in the house of even one of his devotees, and she would count herself richer than any queen. A woman whose heart does not love him is a living corpse — skin and bone dressed in fine clothes — and she had no wish to be such a one. Let her love for him stand, in this world and the next. And as for his words, she did not hold them false: a fickle heart runs after every new thing, but hers, once given, did not wander.

Krishna heard her out, and when she finished he praised her — not her beauty, which every king at the svayamvara had already praised, but her faithfulness, and the vow she had kept. He had seen no wife like her, he said. At her own wedding, with all the kings of the earth gathered to claim her, she had ignored them and sent a brahmin to him in secret. She had never once complained of her brother's enmity, for fear that her words would wound him. She had sent a messenger to win her own husband; she had crossed a kingdom for him. And now, when he teased her, she had believed him — because she could not imagine that he would lie, even in play.

Whatever she desired, he told her, she already held; he was hers, and he wanted nothing more of her. Those who seek him only for the gifts of marriage, he said, are poor in fortune even when rich; but the devotion she had given him, given again and again, was of the kind that sets a soul free from the world.

Then the quiet returned to the chamber, and this time it was the right kind of quiet. The jest was unmade, the tears wiped away, and the two sat together in the peace that follows a storm — the peace of a house where everything has been said and forgiven.

And the old account adds one last thing: as Krishna lived with Rukmini, so he lived in the homes of his other wives — in every house, simply a husband at home.
reflection: Rukmini's long reply never argues with the jest; it simply tells who Krishna is, as if the teasing had asked her to say it aloud. And Krishna's answer is the rarer thing — he praises her not for beauty or rank but for the faithfulness of a choice made against the world.
next_story_tease: Ahead, at a wedding feast in Rukmi's city, a friendly game of dice would end in blood.
